question: Unstable angina and NSTEMI are clinically indistinguishable at the bedside — the diagnosis is made retrospectively by troponin result.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This is actually true. UA and NSTEMI share identical clinical presentations. Serial troponin testing (at 0 and 3 hours with high-sensitivity assays) is the test that separates them — a troponin rise denotes myocardial necrosis (NSTEMI).
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. Both UA and NSTEMI present with ischaemic chest pain at rest, without ST elevation. The distinction requires troponin: if troponin is elevated (above the 99th percentile URL), the diagnosis is NSTEMI; if normal on serial testing, it is UA.
